title: Enhancing Information Literacy through Generative AI in the Library Classroom
extended_summary:
This practice article examines how generative AI chatbots can be incorporated into information literacy instruction for early undergraduate students. The authors focus on the pedagogical challenge of teaching students to use AI tools ethically and critically, especially given concerns about hallucinations, lack of attribution, privacy, and overreliance on AI-generated text. Rather than evaluating a single AI system experimentally, the paper argues for aligning AI use with the ACRL Framework for Information Literacy, especially the frames Scholarship as Conversation, Research as Inquiry, and Searching as Strategic Exploration.

The intervention described is the use of Perplexity AI in two instructional designs: a credit-bearing information literacy course at Weber State University and a first-year chemical engineering classroom activity at Pennsylvania State University. In both cases, AI is used as a scaffold for early-stage research: students generate prompts, review AI-produced summaries, inspect cited sources, evaluate credibility, identify additional keywords, and refine questions. The paper also presents two adaptable classroom assignments, one for a more integrated composition-linked course and one for a single-session subject-specific class.

The population is early undergraduate students in U.S. higher education, with librarians and instructors as the primary implementers. The authors conclude that AI can support research skill development when it is used as a conversational, citation-bearing tool that complements rather than replaces human instruction. They emphasize that the pedagogical value lies in scaffolding and source evaluation, not in AI as a curriculum topic by itself. The paper is primarily a practical framework and instructional position piece, and it recommends future assessment of student outcomes and comparisons of grounded versus ungrounded AI tools.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a practice-oriented article and conceptual classroom report, not a controlled empirical study. It provides descriptive examples and instructor observations, but no rigorous quantitative design, comparison group, or reported statistical analysis.
impact_tier_rationale: The article describes plausible instructional benefits for early undergraduate information literacy, but it offers no measurable effect sizes and no direct evidence of generalizable impact. The likely impact is modest and unclear, based mainly on classroom implementation guidance rather than outcomes data.

interventions.use_case: Using Perplexity AI as a conversational search and research support tool in first-year library and chemical engineering classroom activities, with prompt-based inquiry, source retrieval, summarization, and follow-up questioning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI-supported assignments improved students' information literacy skills, especially source evaluation, keyword development, and understanding scholarly conversation. The authors report instructor-observed improvements in students' research questions being scoped more appropriately and students using retrieved sources in their annotated bibliographies, but no formal quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Information literacy performance in class assignments; quality of research questions, source evaluation, and annotated bibliography use

finding.finding_summary: The assignments were designed to build critical thinking, metacognition, and iterative inquiry through prompt refinement, lateral reading, and source verification. The paper reports that students gained a better sense of the conversation around their topic and improved their ability to narrow or broaden research questions, but the evidence is descriptive rather than experimental.
finding.measure: Critical evaluation, metacognitive reflection, and research-process skills observed in classroom activities

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that Perplexity AI replaced the initial Googling stage with more structured guidance, helping students quickly identify relevant sources and saving class time in both the credit-bearing course and one-session activity. This is presented as improved instructional efficiency and ease of classroom integration, but without measured time-savings data.
finding.measure: Perceived efficiency of research initiation and classroom workflow
